title: Geographic distribution, genetic diversity, and virulence determinants of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli: a descriptive review of the retrieved literature.
abstract: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) is an important foodborne pathogen associated with a wide range of clinical manifestations, from mild gastroenteritis to severe disease. This study aimed to synthesize the evidence retrieved on the reported occurrence and geographic distribution of STEC across different matrices, as well as their genetic diversity, virulence determinants, clinical manifestations, and antimicrobial resistance profiles. A descriptive, non-exhaustive review was conducted based on studies published between 2010 and 2025, resulting in the inclusion of 55 articles after application of the eligibility criteria. The included studies originated from different geographic regions, although the evidence was markedly concentrated in the Americas, particularly Brazil. STEC was investigated across human, animal, food, and environmental sources. Within the retrieved literature, stx2 and stx1 were widely reported, and stx2a, stx2c, and stx2d were among the recurrently reported stx2 subtypes. O157 and non-O157 STEC were both represented across the included studies. These findings describe reporting patterns within the retrieved literature and should not be interpreted as frequencies of occurrence among studies specifically testing each characteristic or as prevalence among STEC isolates. The included studies also reported diverse sequence types and additional virulence determinants, including eae and ehxA. Clinical information was available in only a subset of studies and included manifestations ranging from diarrhea and bloody diarrhea to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Antimicrobial resistance was investigated in a subset of the included studies using phenotypic and/or genotypic approaches. Resistance phenotypes and resistance-associated genetic determinants were reported among STEC isolates in different study populations; however, heterogeneity in analytical populations, antimicrobial panels, testing methods, and reporting approaches precluded overall or pooled estimates of antimicrobial resistance. Overall, the findings highlight the diversity of STEC reported across different sources and geographic settings and reinforce the importance of integrated molecular and epidemiological approaches within a One Health framework.
authors: Gustavo Luis de Paiva Anciens Ramos
journal: Brazilian journal of microbiology : [publication of the Brazilian Society for Microbiology]

title: Measles-like hypermutation of a Newcastle disease virus drives fatal encephalitis during BCMA × CD3 T-cell-redirecting immunotherapy.
abstract: Newcastle disease virus (NDV or AOaV-1) is an avian paramyxovirus that typically causes only mild, self-limiting disease in humans. Here, we report fatal neuroinvasive AOaV-1 infection in a patient with multiple myeloma receiving maintenance therapy with teclistamab, daratumumab, and lenalidomide following frontline teclistamab-based treatment and autologous stem cell transplantation. Following rapidly progressive brainstem-cerebellar encephalitis and negative conventional microbiological testing, unbiased metagenomic RNA sequencing of a cerebellar biopsy identified AOaV-1 at high intraparenchymal abundance. Viral genome analysis revealed striking A-to-G and U-to-C substitutions selectively concentrated in the matrix gene, consistent with ADAR-mediated RNA editing. Long-read sequencing resolved two genetically distinct, independently hypermutated CNS haplotypes. Post-mortem analysis demonstrated widespread dissemination and continued viral diversification in multiple brain regions, whereas a peripheral urine sample contained a minimally mutated putative ancestral lineage. These findings support peripheral infection followed by CNS seeding and compartmentalized within-host evolution. The selective matrix-gene hypermutation closely parallels persistent measles virus infection in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, revealing a shared mechanism of paramyxovirus adaptation to the CNS. Profound immunotherapy-associated immune dysfunction may thus create niches enabling normally low-pathogenic zoonotic viruses to persist, evolve, and acquire severe neurovirulence.

title: Salty virus-host interactions: infection mechanisms of haloarchaeal viruses HRTV-7 and HRTV-10.
abstract: Archaea can be infected by morphologically diverse viruses, and the study of these viruses is important for understanding viral evolution in general. Archaeal tailed viruses make up the largest group of isolated archaeal viruses and the major class of isolated viruses infecting haloarchaea. Yet, little is known about the infection strategies of these viruses. In this study, we focus on archaeal myoviruses and investigate their infection cycles. HRTV-7 and HRTV-10 are both capable of infecting multiple Halorubrum strains, including Halorubrum salinarum B2-2, which is well suited for light microscopy. Virus lifecycle experiments combined with plaque assays and time-lapse microscopy showed that both viruses have a predominantly lytic life cycle, with complete lysis occurring between 9 and 12 h post-infection. Cells swell considerably just prior to lysis, indicating that the cell envelope becomes compromised. Whole-genome sequencing of virus-insensitive strains suggests that HRTV-10 likely uses the S-layer, the main cell envelope component of these archaea, as a receptor. Interestingly, we observed full-length integration of HRTV-7 in virus-resistant cells, as well as parts of the viral genome within the host genome, suggesting viral resistance based on superinfection exclusion. Together, these findings contribute to our understanding of archaeal virus-host interactions and provide insight into their infection strategies.IMPORTANCEViruses of archaea are important to understand the diversity and evolution of all viruses. However, they are little studied. Archaea are ubiquitous microorganisms, of which some thrive at extreme conditions, such as high salt concentrations. Salt-loving haloarchaea are excellent models to study archaeal virus-host interactions due to the high availability of viral isolates and suitability for microscopy. Bacteria and archaea are both infected by tailed viruses; however, in archaea, their infection mechanisms are largely unknown. We used two tailed archaeal viruses infecting the same host to compare their infection strategies. Both viruses induce cell lysis of the host, which is preceded by cell bloating. Interestingly, one of the viruses can integrate into the genome of the host, which renders the strain resistant, suggesting a mechanism of superinfection exclusion. This work provides insight into archaeal virus-host interactions, thereby contributing to the exploration of the unusual archaeal virosphere.

title: Therapeutic and Prophylactic Agents for Viral Diseases: Current Status, Challenges, and Future Prospects.
abstract: Viral diseases remain a major global health challenge despite substantial advances in vaccination, antiviral therapeutics, and public-health interventions. However, current antiviral strategies are still constrained by important gaps, including rapid viral evolution, limited broad-spectrum efficacy, immune escape, antiviral resistance, incomplete durability of protection, and inequitable global access to prevention and treatment. This review provides a comprehensive and integrated overview of contemporary antiviral prevention and therapeutic strategies, spanning vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, direct-acting antivirals, host-targeted therapies, immunomodulators, RNA-based therapeutics, gene-editing technologies, and cellular immunotherapies. We discuss the mechanistic foundations, clinical applications, pharmacologic considerations, and translational challenges associated with each modality across major human viral pathogens, including HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Ebola virus, arboviruses, and herpesviruses. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging innovations such as long-acting prophylaxis, Fc-engineered monoclonal antibodies, nanoparticle and mucosal vaccine platforms, CRISPR-based antiviral systems, and broadly protective host-directed approaches designed to overcome resistance and enhance pandemic preparedness. In addition, we highlight the growing importance of real-time genomic surveillance and equitable global deployment strategies in shaping future antiviral responses, collectively underscoring that the next generation of antiviral medicine will depend on the convergence of universal immunization strategies, durable therapeutics, precision immune modulation, and rapidly deployable platform technologies capable of addressing both endemic and emerging viral threats.

title: The molecular epidemiology of human respiratory syncytial virus in a tertiary paediatric hospital between 2020 and 2024.
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of respiratory illness in young children, contributing significantly to morbidity and mortality and placing a substantial burden on resource-limited healthcare systems. Molecular epidemiological data from sub-Saharan Africa remain limited. This study aimed to investigate the genetic diversity and evolution of RSV in a paediatric population in Cape Town, South Africa, from September 2020 to June 2024. Respiratory syncytial virus-positive respiratory samples with a cycle threshold (Ct) < 30 from patients at Red Cross War Memorial Children's Hospital were sequenced and analysed. Phylogenetic analysis of the partial RSV genome (F and G genes) was conducted using reference sequences derived from a global sequence database. Mutational profiles were assessed for relevance to monoclonal antibody and vaccine effectiveness. Of the 100 selected samples, 42 were sequenced, and 40 had sufficient coverage for analysis. Sequencing failure was associated with higher Ct values, older sample age and suboptimal storage at -20°C. Respiratory syncytial virus-A predominated (78.6%), with A.D.5.1 as the dominant lineage; RSV-B strains (16.7%) clustered within B.D.E.1 and B.D.4.1. Genotypes GA2.3.5 (RSV-A) and GB5.0.5a (RSV-B) were observed, consistent with post-pandemic global trends. G-gene analysis revealed multiple substitutions (G224E, I134K, K262E) suggestive of immune pressure. The F-gene remained more conserved; substitutions such as T122A, S211N and S389P were detected but were not linked to reduced susceptibility to monoclonals. This study demonstrated the co-circulation of genetically diverse RSV-A and RSV-B lineages in children between 2020 and 2024. No established resistance-associated substitutions to currently licensed RSV monoclonal antibodies were identified. Continued genomic surveillance is warranted to monitor RSV evolution. Continued genomic surveillance is essential to strengthen molecular epidemiology and guide public health preparedness.
journal: Journal of the colleges of medicine of South Africa

title: Molecular epidemiology of the RD
abstract: The RDRio genotype of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), a major genotype within the Latin American-Mediterranean (LAM) family, has been associated with increased transmissibility and multidrug resistance (MDR). In Ecuador, a previous baseline study reported a low prevalence of 2.09% for 2012-2016, prior to the large influx of migrants from Venezuela-where RDRio is highly endemic-that has occurred since 2015. This study aimed to update the molecular epidemiology of the RDRio genotype in Ecuador. We screened 699 clinical MTB isolates collected in 2018 (384) and 2023 (315) for the RDRio genotype by duplex PCR and further characterized them by 24-locus MIRU-VNTR typing, spoligotyping, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We conducted minimum spanning tree (MST) analyses based on MIRU-VNTR profiles to assess genetic relatedness. We identified 40 isolates (5.72%) as RDRio, with no significant difference in prevalence between 2018 (n = 20; 5.21%) and 2023 (n = 20; 6.35%). WGS confirmed that the dominant sublineages were 4.3.4.1 and 4.3.4.2, all within Lineage 4 (Euro-American). Genotypic resistance profiling classified 32.1% (9/28) of sequenced isolates as MDR-TB and 7.1% (2/28) as pre-XDR-TB. MST analysis showed that RDRio isolates from Ecuador segregated predominantly into distinct clonal complexes and remained largely isolated from international reference strains, including Venezuelan isolates. The overall RDRio prevalence of 5.72% represents a nearly three-fold increase relative to the 2.09% reported for the 2012-2016 baseline, although it remained stable across the 2018-2023 period and low compared with high-endemicity settings such as Venezuela. Despite this relatively low prevalence, the RDRio genotype was associated with a substantial burden of drug resistance. The genetic segregation of the predominant RDRio Ecuadorian clonal complex from international reference strains-including Venezuelan isolates-did not support recent importation associated with the Venezuelan diaspora. Despite their limitations, classical genotyping methods remain a valid, cost-effective approach to monitor MTB strains of interest associated with MDR-TB, such as RDRio, in low-resource settings like Ecuador.

title: The invisible malaria epidemic in Somalia: why molecular surveillance can no longer wait.
abstract: Malaria remains a hidden public health challenge in Somalia, where weak surveillance systems and reliance on conventional diagnostics may underestimate transmission and disease complexity. The absence of molecular surveillance limits understanding of parasite diversity, drug resistance, and emerging transmission patterns. In the context of climate change, displacement, and fragile health systems, Somalia urgently needs genomic approaches integrated into malaria surveillance. Molecular surveillance can provide critical evidence to strengthen early detection, targeted interventions, and elimination strategies. Establishing these capacities now is essential to prevent an invisible malaria epidemic from becoming an uncontrolled public health crisis.

title: An outbreak of human astrovirus type 5 in a kindergarten in Chongqing, Southwest China.
abstract: On April 20th, 2025, the local Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) received a report regarding several kindergarteners exhibiting symptoms, including vomiting, diarrhoea and fever. Epidemiological investigations and laboratory testing were conducted to identify the causes, formulate preventive and control measures and provide guidance to identify, investigate and manage similar events. An on-site epidemiological investigation was conducted to characterise the clinical and epidemiological features of these cases. Anal swabs from patients and samples from relevant personnel and environmental sources were collected for etiological investigation. The presence of pathogens was confirmed in all anal swabs by multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction test. Genotyping was performed by sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. Nineteen cases met the case definition, with an attack rate of 43.18%. The main clinical manifestations were fever (100%), followed by abdominal pain (68.42%), and diarrhoea (42.11%). Amongst the eight sampled kindergarteners, seven were positive for human astrovirus (HAstV). Whole-genome sequencing and bioinformatics analysis revealed that the outbreak strain belonged to genotype 5 and the strain sequences of the positive cases were highly homologous (p distance < 0.001). Phylogenetic analysis showed that this strain was closely related to the previously prevalent HAstV-5 strain isolated from Fuzhou, China in 2013 (GenBank accession no. MF684776.1). No gene recombination events were found. According to the laboratory test results, HAstV-5 was the aetiological agent of the outbreak. Further research focusing on enhanced surveillance strategies and improved diagnostic tools is required to guide the identification, investigation and management of HAstV outbreaks. Not applicable.

title: Genome mining and comprehensive molecular characterization of feline Panleukopenia virus reveals distinct VP2 mutational signatures and evolutionary divergence.
abstract: Feline Panleukopenia Virus is a highly contagious, systemic, and environmentally stable virus that primarily targets leukocytes and affects cats of all ages. Despite its clinical and epidemiological importance, limited molecular surveillance studies have been conducted in the densely populated downstate region of New York. The objective of this study was to investigate the molecular and serological prevalence of FPV among shelter cats in this region and to isolate and genetically characterize circulating strains. Samples, including swabs and sera, were collected from 108 shelter cats and tested using quantitative PCR (qPCR) and immunofluorescent assay (IFA), respectively. Results showed that 25.0% (27/108) of the cats were FPV-positive by qPCR, while 39.8% (43/108) were positive by IFA, indicating active viral circulation within the tested populations. Viral isolation was successfully performed using Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) cells. Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) confirmed the detection of a newly characterized FPV isolate (Accession: PZ251627) circulating within the tested shelter cat population. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated high nucleotide similarity with previously reported FPV strains, including MH165482 (99.3%), MN127781 (99.2%), and MH165481 (99.2%). Analysis of the VP2 gene also revealed close similarity with isolates OQ615264, KT899746, and PVMRFD, along with two amino acid substitutions, Ile101Thr and Glu411Ala. Spatial interpolation analysis identified a higher occurrence of FPV-positive cats in western downstate New York, emphasizing the importance of continued surveillance and monitoring programs.
journal: Infection, genetics and evolution : journal of molecular epidemiology and evolutionary genetics in infectious diseases

title: Molecular surveillance, serotyping, antimicrobial profiling, and pathogenicity of multidrug-resistant Salmonella enterica isolated from broiler chickens in upper Egypt.
abstract: Salmonella enterica remains a major threat to poultry production and public health owing to its zoonotic potential and the increasing emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains. However, comprehensive data integrating the molecular epidemiology, serotype diversity, antimicrobial resistance, and pathogenicity of circulating Salmonella strains in Upper Egypt remain limited. Therefore, this study investigated the molecular characteristics, serotype distribution, antimicrobial resistance, and pathogenicity of Salmonella enterica isolated from broiler chickens across seven governorates in Upper Egypt. A total of 350 clinical samples from diseased broilers were examined using conventional bacteriological methods and invA-based PCR. Confirmed isolates were subjected to serotyping, partial gene sequencing, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) determination, and experimental pathogenicity evaluation in 3-day-old SPF broiler chicks. Conventional bacteriology recovered 150 presumptive isolates (42.86%), whereas 80 isolates (22.86%) were confirmed by invA PCR. Serotyping of 20 confirmed isolates identified eight serovars belonging to five serogroups, with S. Enteritidis (35%) and S. Typhimurium (25%) predominating. Multidrug resistance (MDR) was detected in 95% (19/20) of the serotyped Salmonella isolates, exhibiting high Multiple Antibiotic Resistance (MAR) indices, including complete resistance to amoxicillin and cephradine and 80% resistance to colistin sulfate. Experimental infection confirmed the high pathogenicity of both MDR field strains, resulting in cumulative morbidity rates of 80.0% and 86.7% and mortality rates of 26.7% and 33.3% for S. Enteritidis and S. Typhimurium, respectively. Both serovars significantly reduced body weight (P < 0.05), while S. Typhimurium produced more severe growth retardation, diarrhea, depression, and hepatic lesions (P < 0.05). In contrast, S. Enteritidis caused significantly greater yolk sac and cardiac lesions (P < 0.05), indicating distinct serovar-specific tissue tropism. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the circulation of genetically diverse, multidrug-resistant, and highly pathogenic Salmonella enterica strains in broiler chickens in Upper Egypt, emphasizing the need for continuous molecular surveillance, strengthened biosecurity, and prudent antimicrobial stewardship to mitigate economic losses and reduce the zoonotic risk of salmonellosis.
